title: Entanglement Scaling and Problem Structure in Quantum Approximate and Adiabatic Optimization Algorithms
authors: Georgios Arapantonis, Paraj Titum, Gregory Quiroz
abstract: Entanglement is widely regarded as a key resource underlying the power of quantum algorithms and their potential to achieve quantum advantage. With the emergence of variational quantum algorithms, however, questions have arisen regarding how entanglement relates to problem structure and algorithmic performance in near-term quantum applications. Here, we examine this relationship through the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA), a specific class of variational algorithms, applied to the MaxCut problem. We show that suboptimal variational parameter training can significantly modify the observed entanglement profile, obscuring its scaling behavior. By employing a high-performance optimizer, we find empirical evidence that QAOA exhibits entanglement scaling consistent with that of fermionic Gaussian states (up to a scaling factor) across a broad range of MaxCut instances. We further compare these results with adiabatic quantum computation, observing annealing-schedule-dependent entanglement profiles whose scaling behavior differs markedly from that of QAOA. Together, these findings provide new insight into how entanglement manifests in and distinguishes these two algorithmic paradigms, highlighting its connection to both computational performance and application structure.
summary: This paper rigorously compares the entanglement scaling between QAOA and AQC when solving MaxCut on various graphs. It demonstrates that while both methods show volume-law scaling, their specific entanglement profiles differ based on the algorithm's structure and the annealing schedule chosen. The findings establish a strong link between quantum resource theory (entanglement) and the fundamental performance characteristics of near-term quantum algorithms.
main_problem: The paper investigates how entanglement scaling relates to problem structure when comparing two major quantum optimization paradigms: QAOA and AQC, applied to the MaxCut problem.
main_result: QAOA exhibits entanglement scaling consistent with fermionic Gaussian states under optimal parameter training, while AQC shows distinct, schedule-dependent entanglement profiles. The study highlights that classical optimization protocols significantly impact the observed entanglement profile in variational algorithms.
method: The authors use numerical simulations to calculate and compare entanglement entropy across various bipartitions for QAOA and AQC applied to MaxCut on different graph structures (k-regular, complete).
model_or_system: The system is modeled using qubits encoding the MaxCut problem Hamiltonian ($H_C$). The algorithms analyzed are the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) and Adiabatic Quantum Computation (AQC), which operate in a Hilbert space of dimension $2^N$.
key_observables: Entanglement entropy ($S$), approximation ratio ($r$), required entanglement ($	ext{S}_{	ext{req}}$), and the peak depth ($p^*$) at which maximum entanglement is reached.
important_parameters: QAOA depth ($p$), graph edge density ($\alpha$), system size ($N$), and the specific annealing schedule function $f(s)$ for AQC.
main_assumptions: The analysis often relies on sampling an ensemble of bipartitions to estimate average entanglement entropy, which is assumed accurate enough for scaling studies. It also compares results against analytical bounds like the Page Value and FGS estimates.
figures_summary: Figures compare required entanglement ($	ext{S}_{	ext{req}}$) vs. depth ($p$) or edge density ($\alpha$) across different graph types (k-regular, complete), contrasting QAOA/AQC behavior with theoretical benchmarks like fermionic Gaussian states.
paper_structure: The paper systematically compares the entanglement scaling of QAOA and AQC for MaxCut on various graphs, detailing how initialization strategies affect results, establishing connections to FGS bounds, and analyzing the dependence of AQC entanglement on the annealing schedule path.
why_interesting: This work provides deep insights into the resource theory aspect of quantum computation by quantifying exactly *how* much entanglement is required and generated by different algorithmic approaches for optimization problems.

Panels (a) and (b) present the average Sp(N/2; N) as a function of QAOA depth p for informed and random initialization, respectively. Panels (c) and (d) show the corresponding approximation ratios. Re- sults are averaged over 50 random instances of weighted complete graphs. Error bars indicate the standard error of the mean and are too small to be visible in panels (a) and (b). The performance of the classical optimizer can affect the entanglement profile of complete graphs.

FIG. 3. Scaling of Sreq(N/2; N) in QAOA for Datasets KR and CW. SP (N/2; N) and SG(N/2; N) denote analytical predictions for Haar random states (i.e. Page Value) and fermionic Gaussian states, respectively; see Sec. V C for further details. Error bars denote the standard error of the mean and are smaller than the marker size. The required entanglement is upper-bounded by that of fermionic Gaussian states and scales linearly with system size for both training schemes implemented in this work.

FIG. 4. Numerical simulations for entanglement requirement of QAOA for arbitrary graphs. Results from Dataset KR (circles) and Datasets CW and ED (squares) are shown. Panel (a) shows results, normalized by complete graphs, as a function of edge density. Dashed lines indicate the linear fit described in the text. Panel (b) shows Sp(N/2; N) versus QAOA depth for N = 10 qubits with different edge counts. Error bars denote the standard error of the mean. The fit accurately captures the entanglement in the high edge-density regime.

FIG. 5. Numerical simulations for the entanglement requirement in QAOA, across all bipartitions and different graph families. Data for (a) k-regular graphs from Dataset KR and (b) complete graphs and graphs with varying edges from Datasets CW, ED are shown. Differ- ent colors reflect the edge density, while different markers indicate the system size. Error bars denote the standard error of the mean. For graphs with large edge density, the numerical data collapse onto a single curve, which is well described by Eq. (19).
